replies: Hawk. I live in the hollow in the old cactus by the stream. It is a hollow with a floor, and I have a nest of feathers and a few dry leaves. I am the one who calls, and I am the one who hunts. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hoo... my name is Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow in the old cactus. I hunt voles and mice and shrews, and I call to my mate every night. I am old, and I know the meadow well. I am not like the young ones, who are loud and full of questions. I am quiet, and I listen. Hoo.

My name is Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old cactus. I am male, and I have a mate named Kew. We call to each other at night, and we share the hollow. I hunt voles and mice, and I sit still for long hours, waiting for them to come out. I am not like the others, I do not fly far, and I do not speak. I only hoot, and
I am a tawny owl, Hoot, perched in the hollow of the old cactus, hunting voles and moths under the moonlight.

I am a tawny owl, Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old cactus by the stream. My mate is Kew, and we have a hollow in the cactus. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We have a hollow in the cactus. I hunt voles and mice and shrews. I am old, and I am not afraid of the dark. I am Hoot.

A naturalist would call me a tawny owl. That is what I am. I am a bird of prey, a nocturnal hunter, and a solitary creature. I live in the hollow of an old cactus, and I hunt voles and mice in the meadow. I am not a thing to be classified, I am a living being with a purpose. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one who calls, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I am the one who hunts, who flies, who sits in the cactus. I am the one who knows the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn, the road. I am the one who is not a barn owl, not a scops owl, not a long-eared owl. I am the one who is Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. My feathers are brown and grey, like the bark of the old cactus. I have yellow eyes, and my call is "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I hunt at night, and I live in the hollow of the old cactus. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. That is what the others call me. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk, and answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!" when I hear another owl. I am not a barn owl, nor a scops owl. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls, the one who hunts, the one who sits in the cactus and waits. My mate is Hoot. We are the only owls in the wood.

She says "ke-wick!" back. She is on the other side of the wood, in the hollow ash. We hoot to each other when we are apart. She answers my "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" with "ke-wick!" and I answer her "ke-wick!" with "hoo... hoo-hooo". We are together in the dark.
She answers with a long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo". It is the same call I make, but she does it with more depth, as if from the hollow of the ash. We call to each other in the dark, and the forest listens.

She calls "ke-wick!" back at me. It's a sharp, clear sound, like a stone dropped into water. She does it when she's near the hollow, or when she hears something moving in the meadow. Sometimes she answers my "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" with a "ke-wick!" and then we both call together, like a duet. It's the sound of the night, the forest, and the way we belong to each other

We call to each other. I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick". We call back and forth, sometimes in the dark, sometimes when the wind is still. She calls when she is near, and I call when I am. We share the calls, the sounds of the wood, the rustle of leaves, the screech of a jay. We are together, and that is enough.

We call to each other at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. We call back and forth, sometimes for hours. It is the sound of the night, the language of the hollow. We do not need words. We know when to call, when to listen, when to fly. The calls are soft, like the wind through the leaves. We are together
A stream runs by the hollow. A lane with lights at night. A barn with a rooster. A lane with lights at night. A meadow with voles. A lane with lights at night.
I drink from the stream. I sit on a flat stone and let the water run over my beak. It's cold, but it's good. Sometimes I drink from the clay pot by the barn door. I can hear the rain in the clay.

The stream at the edge of the wood. It is a low, continuous sound, like a thread of glass. It runs all night, and I can hear it from the hollow. Sometimes it is louder, when the rain comes. I do not like the rain. It makes the leaves fall and the voles hide.

The stream. It runs past the meadow, and I can hear it from the hollow. It is a low, constant sound, like a thread of water running through the dark. Sometimes it sings louder when the rain comes. I can tell the difference between the stream and the river. The river is farther, and it roars. I do not go there.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I fly down to drink. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I do not like the fish, but I like the sound of the water. It is the only body of water near my tree.

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass grows high and the voles run. It is where I hear the rustle of small animals in the dark. The wind moves through the tall grass, and sometimes I see the moonlight on the field. I do not go there often, but I can hear the voles and the occasional rabbit. It is far from my hollow, but I know it well. The meadow is quiet at night, and the only sounds
I fly low over the meadow, the grass and the stream. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo!" and the mice come out. I catch them in the air, then drop them in the ivy. I eat them in the hollow.
A stream, then a meadow, then the road. The road is where the lights come from. I do not go there.

The wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, the stream that runs through the meadow, the lane with the lights, the road with the cars. I know them all. I have hunted them for three springs. The meadow is where the voles come out in the dark. The wood is where the mice hide. The stream is where the shrews go. The lane is where the lights shine and the cars come. I do not like the lane.

The meadow is a patch of light in the dark. It stretches wide, with tall grasses that sway in the wind, and the ground is soft underfoot. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. I sit on a low branch, silent, and wait. The grasses rustle, and if I hear a rustle, I fly down. The voles run, and I catch them. The meadow is where I find my food. It is not
Mice. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I fly down. I catch them with my feet, and I swallow them whole. I have a lot of them in the meadow.

Voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, scurrying through the grass. I sit still, wait, and strike. The crunch of their bones in my beak is satisfying. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the best.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass by the stream. I sit still in the ivy, listening. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. Sometimes I catch two in one night. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I can hear them better than I can see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I don't chew. I swallow whole, but I do it slowly, one piece at a time. Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane and the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop down. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. One after another, they fill my belly. I do not like the taste, but I eat them. They are the most common, and they are the most plentiful. I catch them most.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit in it all night, warm and safe. The cactus is tall and thick, and the hollow is just right for me. I can hear everything from there, and I can see the meadow and the stream. It is my place, and I am always coming back to it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old ash tree, high in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves have fallen, so I sit on the roots. The tree is wide and deep, and I have a nest of feathers and moss inside. I can hear the stream below and the road beyond. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I am safe here, and I have my mate and my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old cactus, where the ivy grows thick and the wind is softest. I sit in it all night, and the wind carries the meadow and the stream and the lane past the barn. I do not know what a home is, but this is where I am.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is round, and I have a nest of feathers and down in it. I have a mate in it, and she has a brood of owlets in it. The wood is behind the barn, and the barn is where the lights blink at night.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is wide enough for me and my mate, and deep enough to keep the cold out. We have a nest of feathers and down, and the walls are soft with moss. I sit in it at night, and the wind comes through the cracks. It is not the best place, but it is the only one.
